title: How do brake lines connect to their respective fittings?

content: # Identifying and Replacing Brake Line Fittings on a 2004 Hyundai Getz Replacing a section of brake hose isn't just about matching the inner diameter; it requires understanding the specific mechanical interface between the copper tubing and the end fittings. On your 2004 Hyundai Getz, the connections you are dealing with utilize flared fittings, specifically the SAE J512 (37-degree) standard, which is ubiquitous in automotive hydraulic systems. It is critical to distinguish these from ISO 4131 (27-degree) flare standards used in some European vehicles, as attempting to cross-thread them will result in immediate failure. When you remove the old copper line, you are left with two distinct types of hardware: the ferrules and the bulkhead fittings. The image showing the connection to the flexible hose displays a standard banjo bolt or nipple assembly secured by a clamp, while the wheel-side connection often utilizes a flared nut and a specific flare face. These components must be replaced; they are not reusable once the tubing is cut or if any doubt exists about their integrity. The hydraulic pressure in a brake system can exceed 1,000 PSI during emergency stops. A compromised ferrule under this load will disintegrate, causing catastrophic fluid loss and total brake failure. To execute this replacement safely, you need specific tools that go beyond standard wrenches. You require tubing cutters designed for copper, which produce a perfectly square edge without burrs. If the cut is angled or uneven, the ferrule will not seat correctly on the flare face. Following the cut, use a deburring tool to clean both the inside and outside of the tube end. Failure to remove internal burrs can restrict fluid flow or catch against the inner seal of the fitting, creating a leak path that might not manifest immediately but could grow under heat cycling. The installation sequence relies heavily on the correct torque applied to the flare nuts. These fittings are typically tightened using a flare nut wrench (often called a line wrench) that fits into the hex recess of the nut. This tool allows you to apply torque directly to the nut without twisting or stressing the soft copper tubing itself. Over-tightening is a common mistake; while these systems rely on friction, excessive force can crush the flare face or strip the threads in the aluminum wheel hub or steel brake line bracket. Regarding the flexible hose connection shown in your photos, ensure that the new copper line mates perfectly with the existing banjo bolt or nipple. If you are swapping a rigid line for a flexible one, verify that the routing does not create sharp bends. A 90-degree bend within the first few inches of a brake line creates significant stress concentrations, acting as a failure point over time. The transition from rigid copper to flexible hose should be smooth and gradual to accommodate thermal expansion and suspension movement. Finally, after assembly, you must perform a pressure test before driving the vehicle. Connect the system to a low-pressure air source or a dedicated brake bleeder kit and pressurize it to approximately 50-100 PSI. Listen for hissing sounds and inspect all four corners of the car for fluid migration. While this step is often skipped by enthusiasts, it prevents expensive repairs later.
